lessons.title: अगर … तो … (agar … to …) — if, then
lessons.gloss: if …, then … — a condition and what follows from it

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say "if". (अगर, agar.) Then open a reply with "so, then": तो चलिए. The two words meet in this lesson.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: अगर … तो … with the future

segments.text: अगर बारिश होगी, तो हम घर पर रहेंगे। agar bāriś hogī, to ham ghar par raheṅge. — "If it rains, we will stay at home."
अगर opens the condition and तो opens what follows from it. When both halves are still to come, Hindi puts both in the future: होगी, रहेंगे. English says "if it rains"; Hindi says "if it will rain".
अगर तुम आओगे, तो मुझे अच्छा लगेगा। (agar tum āoge, to mujhe acchā lagegā.) — If you come, I'll be glad.
Keep both words: अगर at the start, तो at the turn.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: if it is so now

segments.text: अगर तुम्हें भूख लगी है, तो खाना खाओ। agar tumhẽ bhūkh lagī hai, to khānā khāo. — "If you're hungry, eat."
When the condition is true now, it stays in the present, and the second half can ask, advise or tell:
अगर समय है, तो आइए। (agar samay hai, to āie.) — If you have time, do come.
अगर आप बीमार हैं, तो आपको आराम करना चाहिए। (agar āp bīmār haiṁ, to āpko ārām karnā cāhiye.) — If you're ill, you should rest.

अगर बारिश होगी, तो मैं घर पर रहूँगा। अगर तुम्हें भूख लगी है, तो खाना खाओ।

feedback.correct: The future in both halves for what is still to come; the present for what is true now.
feedback.incorrect: agar opens, to turns: agar bāriś hogī, to …; for now, agar tumhẽ bhūkh lagī hai, to ….

segments.text: Which word opens the condition? (अगर.) Which opens what follows? (तो.) "If it rains, we will stay at home"? (अगर बारिश होगी, तो हम घर पर रहेंगे: the future in both halves.) "If you're hungry, eat"? (अगर तुम्हें भूख लगी है, तो खाना खाओ.)

lessons.title: अगर ट्रेन छूट गई, तो … (agar ṭren chūṭ gaī, to …) — if it happens, and otherwise
lessons.gloss: if the train is missed, then … — the plain past after अगर, and otherwise

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say "I missed my train". (मेरी ट्रेन छूट गई.) Then "if it rains, we will stay at home". (अगर बारिश होगी, तो हम घर पर रहेंगे.)

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the plain past after अगर

segments.text: अगर मेरी ट्रेन छूट गई, तो मैं बस से आऊँगा। agar merī ṭren chūṭ gaī, to maiṁ bas se āūṅgā. — "If I miss my train, I'll come by bus."

For one event that may or may not happen, Hindi can put it in the plain past after अगर, as if it had already happened: छूट गई. The result stays in the future. It is the past of a story, used to try a case out.
अगर आपको देर हो गई, तो मुझे फ़ोन कीजिए। (agar āpko der ho gaī, to mujhe fon kījiye.) — If you're running late, phone me.
अगर उसने हाँ कहा, तो हम कल चलेंगे। (agar usne hā̃ kahā, to ham kal caleṅge.) — If she says yes, we'll go tomorrow.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: नहीं तो, otherwise

segments.text: जल्दी चलो, नहीं तो देर हो जाएगी। jaldī calo, nahīṃ to der ho jāegī. — "Hurry up, otherwise we'll be late."

नहीं तो (nahīṃ to) is "if not, then": a warning about what follows if the first part does not happen. The first part is often a request. The warning is in the future: here हो जाएगी, the future of हो गई.
खाना खाओ, नहीं तो भूख लगेगी। (khānā khāo, nahīṃ to bhūkh lagegī.) — Eat, or you'll get hungry.

acceptedResponses: agar merī ṭren chūṭ gaī, to maiṁ bas se āūṅgā; jaldī calo, nahīṃ to der ho jāegī
अगर मेरी ट्रेन छूट गई, तो मैं बस से आऊँगा। जल्दी चलो, नहीं तो देर हो जाएगी।

feedback.correct: chūṭ gaī tries the case out; the result and the warning are in the future.
feedback.incorrect: After agar, the plain past: chūṭ gaī; then to and the future. For the warning, nahīṃ to and the future.

segments.text: "If I miss my train"? (अगर मेरी ट्रेन छूट गई.) Which tense goes in the result? (The future.) "Otherwise"? (नहीं तो.) "We'll be late"? (देर हो जाएगी.)

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Before the new one: say "hurry up, otherwise we'll be late". (जल्दी चलो, नहीं तो देर हो जाएगी.)
वरना — varnā — "otherwise, or else".
जल्दी उठो, वरना ट्रेन छूट जाएगी। jaldī uṭho, varnā ṭren chūṭ jāegī. — "Get up early, or you'll miss the train."
It does the work of नहीं तो in one word, and stands in the same place, before the warning.
धीरे बोलो, वरना बच्चा जाग जाएगा। (dhīre bolo, varnā baccā jāg jāegā.) — Speak softly, or the child will wake up.
वरना (varnā) is usually traced to Persian varna, "otherwise". It ends like a Hindi verb in -ना, but it is not one, and it never changes.
